question: What is the main reason we track germs and diseases in healthcare (microbial surveillance)?

options.A: Managing hospital financial budgets and staff salaries
options.B: Treating individual patients with chronic illnesses
options.C: Tracking health data to detect and monitor disease patterns
options.D: Conducting laboratory research on plant genetics

explanation: Spot-on! Surveillance is all about keeping an eye on how pathogens move so we can protect our communities. You've got this! [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h1)

question: Why is it so important to keep collecting health data on a daily basis?

options.A: It guarantees immediate funding from international organizations
options.B: It completely eliminates all infectious diseases from communities
options.C: It allows workers to anticipate outbreaks before they escalate
options.D: It replaces the need for direct patient bedside nursing care

explanation: Exactly! Continuous tracking gives us an early warning, helping us stop outbreaks before they turn into full-blown emergencies. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h1)

question: Which of these is a major goal of public health surveillance?

options.A: Diagnose individual patients in emergency departments
options.B: Provide personal insurance for hospital staff
options.C: Manufacture essential vaccines and pharmaceutical drugs
options.D: Measure disease burden and identify high-risk populations

explanation: Spot on! Surveillance helps us see how heavy a disease's impact is and figure out who is most at risk so we can help them. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h2)

question: What usually happens when health programs don't have reliable surveillance data to work with?

options.A: Disease outbreaks resolve much faster automatically
options.B: Patient compliance with treatment plans increases significantly
options.C: Hospitals receive surplus funding and medical supplies
options.D: Interventions rely on guesswork instead of concrete evidence

explanation: Correct! Without good data, we are just guessing. Reliable figures help us put resources where they are truly needed. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h2)

question: How does 'passive surveillance' usually work in a healthcare setting?

options.A: Clinicians routinely report diagnosed cases to central authorities
options.B: Public health staff actively search clinics for hidden cases
options.C: International agencies take over local hospital management
options.D: Patients diagnose themselves at home without laboratory tests

explanation: Well done! In passive surveillance, we wait for hospitals and clinics to send in their regular reports of diagnosed cases. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h3)

question: Public health officers visit local clinics to actively search for missed cholera cases. What type of surveillance is this?
explanation: Spot on! When health workers go out looking for cases instead of waiting for reports to come in, that's active surveillance. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h3)

question: Why do we use standardized case definitions when tracking diseases?

options.A: They eliminate the need for any laboratory confirmation
options.B: They ensure consistent reporting criteria across different regions
options.C: They reduce the cost of purchasing hospital equipment
options.D: They prevent patients from seeking traditional medical care

explanation: Correct! Standard definitions mean every clinic and state is counting the exact same thing the exact same way. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h4)

question: Which of these modern tools do health workers commonly use to record patient data easily?

options.B: Mobile health applications and electronic records
options.C: Intravenous infusion pumps and oxygen cylinders
options.D: Surgical scalpels and sterile dressing forceps

explanation: You got it! Digital tools and phone apps help make data collection much faster and more accurate. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h4)

question: Why are nurses in a great position to help with microbial surveillance?

options.A: They manage national government health budgets directly
options.B: They manufacture all vaccines used in public hospitals
options.C: They assess patients first and notice subtle clinical shifts
options.D: They hold exclusive authority to declare national epidemics

explanation: Exactly! Because nurses spend the most time at the bedside, they are usually the first to notice when something unusual is happening. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h5)

question: A staff nurse notices a sudden jump in wound infections on the surgical ward. What should be done first?

options.A: Discharge all current surgical patients immediately
options.B: Wait until the end of the month to mention it
options.C: Notify the infection control team and document findings
options.D: Prescribe broad-spectrum antibiotics without a doctor

explanation: Spot on! Quick reporting helps the infection control team step in early and stop a potential outbreak in the ward. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h5)

question: What is usually the very first step when surveillance data shows a sudden spike in infections?

options.A: Close down the entire national health ministry
options.B: Confirm the diagnosis and verify the outbreak
options.C: Destroy all available laboratory testing supplies
options.D: Stop keeping medical records for new patients

explanation: Well done! Before sounding full alarm bells, we always need to make sure the lab results are verified and it's a real outbreak. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h6)

question: During a cholera outbreak, what is a very practical role for a nurse in the response team?

options.A: Designing blueprints for new municipal water pipes
options.B: Tracing contacts and educating communities on hygiene
options.C: Importing foreign medication without regulatory approval
options.D: Conducting political campaigns for health ministers

explanation: Correct! Nurses are brilliant educators; teaching proper hygiene and tracking contacts are key ways we beat outbreaks. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h6)

question: Which of these is a major challenge for disease surveillance in resource-limited health systems?

options.A: Excessive funding that overwhelms local bank accounts
options.B: Instantaneous internet access in every rural village
options.C: Limited laboratory infrastructure and power supply issues
options.D: An overwhelming surplus of highly trained epidemiologists

explanation: Spot on. Bad power supply and lacking lab facilities make it really tough to test samples and store vaccines properly. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h7)

question: How does extreme staff burnout affect public health surveillance data?

options.A: It eliminates all errors in patient disease diagnosis
options.B: It guarantees perfect electronic record keeping daily
options.C: It leads to under-reporting and skewed data accuracy
options.D: It increases the speed of laboratory specimen processing

explanation: Exactly. When nurses and doctors are overworked and exhausted, reporting cases slips through the cracks, leading to messy data. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h7)
